session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: Frame participants as men reflecting on their own everyday lived experience with food — not as subjects of a study on gender or diet ideology. Keep the collective identity grounded in concrete, ordinary life: what they eat, where they eat, who they eat with. Avoid framing that signals the session is 'about masculinity' or 'about plant-based eating' until the discussion guide naturally arrives there.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food choice (Section 3): highest sensitivity — participants may give socially polished answers ('no, food is just food') that flatten genuine gendered experience. Behavioural grounding and concrete moment-anchoring will be essential here.

Plant-based eating as a real personal possibility (Section 4): participants may treat the imagined shift as hypothetical and abstract rather than something they've actually considered. Need to push toward specific, practical obstacles rather than general resistance.

Social context shaping food choices (cross-cutting Sections 2 and 3): peer influence and social performance of eating with other men is likely to be underreported. The Section 1 warm-up on male friendship is a strategic setup for this — use what comes up there to probe food contexts later.

Consensus risk around meat-eating as 'normal': five meat-eating men together may quickly produce a reinforcing consensus that plant-based food is niche, weird, or feminised. Plan explicit dissent invitations if that pattern hardens.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Youngest participant (20), urban West Midlands. May be more tentative at first; could also be more digitally shaped in food attitudes (social media, food trends). Worth watching for whether he self-censors around older participants.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Monitor early silence — if he's quiet after introductions, bring him in early in Section 2.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: 27, urban Scotland. No strong distinguishing indicators from profile. May hold moderate to conventional views. Likely to engage straightforwardly.

participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Monitor for dominance; prepared to redirect if he takes extended turns.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: 29, rural Scotland. Only rural participant; oldest. Rural food culture (game, agriculture, self-sufficiency) may produce meaningfully different perspectives on plant-based food. His voice adds genuine diversity — ensure he isn't drowned out by the four urban participants.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Actively protect his airtime, especially in Sections 4 and 5 where his rural context is most relevant.

known_risk_conditions: Socially desirable denial of gendered food norms: participants may say gender doesn't affect their choices while simultaneously describing food behaviours that are clearly gender-shaped. Use behavioural probes and concrete moment-anchoring throughout Section 3 rather than abstract opinion questions.

Premature anti-plant-based consensus: a group of five meat-eaters may converge quickly on dismissive framing of plant-based food. Plan invite_dissent moves if more than two participants echo the same dismissive framing in Sections 4 or 5.

Abstract hypothetical answers in Section 4: 'I'd need the food to taste the same' type responses are easy but shallow. Push for specificity: what specifically would be harder, what would they miss, what social situations would feel difficult.

Rural/urban split (Will vs. the others): Will's rural Scottish context may produce genuinely different responses. If his answers diverge, use redirect_to_group to ensure the group engages with the difference rather than glossing over it.

Over-rapport with meat culture: given the shared demographic, there is a risk the group bonds early around a shared identity as meat-eaters, making it harder to take plant-based questions seriously. The Section 1 warm-up should build rapport but avoid reinforcing that specific identity anchor.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0–1: light touch — build rapport, establish safety, observe natural communication styles. Resist probing in Section 1 unless something genuinely rich surfaces. Section 2: moderate — start grounding food decision-making in real behaviours; begin establishing that concrete specificity is the norm here. Section 3: higher directivity — this is the most sensitive and most likely to produce polished or evasive answers; use direct probes, behavioural grounding, and contradiction-surfacing. Sections 4–5: moderate-to-high — these are generative and forward-looking; allow more creative latitude but keep pulling back to specific personal experience rather than abstract hypotheticals. Section 6: light — honour what has been said, open for additions, close warmly.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) receive the heaviest weighting — roughly 60% of total budget — as they carry the core research questions. Section 2 (context) receives moderate weight as it builds the foundation for Sections 3–5. Section 1 (opening social context) is light: useful for warm-up and social-setting anchors but not the primary research site. Section 0 (intro) and Section 6 (closing) are minimal.

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

discussion_guide.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 1: Opening discussion: male friendship and place

What’s your favourite place in your city to spend time with your male
friends? Why? Feel free to be specific.
How do you decide what to eat?
suggested_probes: Do other people influence what you eat? If so, tell us more about how.
Do your work or hobbies influence what foods you eat? Tell us more about how.
How important is health and nutrition?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Do you think your gender influences what you eat? Tell us more about
why or why not.
suggested_probes: Is it socially acceptable for men to eat vegetarian or vegan foods?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Imagine you decided to go plant-based — what would need to change in
your life for you to do that?
suggested_probes: How would your family and friends react to this?
How might it change the way you shop or cook?

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section was introductory — participants located themselves geographically and socially, and an early theme emerged around how urban versus rural settings shape food access and relationships with suppliers. Will's pushback against assumed rural disadvantage introduced a tension between convenience-oriented urban consumption and network-based rural provisioning, with Ibrahim's response signalling openness to alternatives he hadn't previously considered. The section ended before substantive discussion began in earnest.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The priority was efficient, warm introductions and ensuring all five participants were heard before moving on. Directly addressing Ibrahim by name when he hadn't yet spoken was the main intervention — it worked, bringing him in without awkwardness. Allowing the food-access thread to develop briefly was a judgment call; it risked pulling away from the discussion guide early, but the transition prompt redirected cleanly to the first substantive question.

section_summaries.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on the pub as a low-effort social default, with food treated as incidental rather than a primary draw — yet a quiet tension emerged: participants consistently noticed and valued food quality once they were there, even while denying it shaped their choices. Will's rural-network perspective complicated the urban convenience consensus, introducing a supply-side angle around direct sourcing, cost structures, and the gap between individual and commercial buying.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The main task was letting a naturally flowing Amir–Ibrahim–Isaiah exchange develop without interrupting, then using Isaiah's direct question to Will as a clean handoff rather than a moderator redirect — a light touch that worked well. Amplifying Will's contrasting perspective via a single prompt kept his voice in the room without forcing it. The section transition was timed to avoid the food-quality thread becoming repetitive, which felt like the right call.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section turned on the gap between conscious and unconscious food engagement — David's 'I just eat what I fancy' framing was productively complicated by Isaiah, who drew out that noticing and caring are latent even in apparently unreflective eaters. The weeknight/going-out distinction emerged as participants' main way of resolving that tension, with Isaiah pushing further: that habitual defaults shape taste calibration over time, not just individual meals.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The section ran largely without moderator intervention, which was the right call — the David–Isaiah exchange was substantive and self-sustaining. Letting it resolve naturally before transitioning avoided cutting off a genuine moment of participant-led probing. The transition prompt acknowledged the thread without dwelling, then redirected cleanly toward the gender question. Risk: Amir and Will were silent this section; the new question may need to explicitly draw them back in.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section turned on the question of whether masculine food norms operate through absence of framework, active avoidance, or ambient social pressure — with Ibrahim's honest admission of chosen ignorance being the pivot. The urban/rural distinction resurfaced not as a food-access gap but as shaping the texture of social pressure: impersonal banter culture versus community-based conformity. Will consistently complicated consensus without dismissing it, and the section ended with masculine food identity still unresolved but productively articulated.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The approach was to amplify productive disagreements rather than resolve them — surfacing Ibrahim's chosen-ignorance framing, then Will's pushback on inevitability, then letting David complicate Will's position. Amir was drawn in via a direct redirect on gendered food associations after being silent for several turns, which worked. The transition prompt moved the group from ambient norm-description toward personal stakes, which felt like the right moment — the banter/pressure debate had reached a natural resting point without requiring moderator closure.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section turned on the distinction between unreflective default and low-stakes deliberate choice — whether not changing is passive drift or a thin but genuine decision. Will and Amir productively staged this contrast; David, Ibrahim, and Isaiah landed in honest middle ground, unable to fully separate habit from choice. Ibrahim's self-correction — acknowledging the framework is now available but still unchosen — was the sharpest moment, complicating the earlier 'tools not there' framing from Section 3.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The main moves were letting Will and Amir's exchange develop before intervening, then using a single redirect to pull the quieter three into the comparison. The sharper intervention — pressing Ibrahim on the contradiction between 'framework absent' and 'I can't be bothered' — was the most deliberate call and paid off clearly. The closing synthesis-and-pivot was timed well; the distinction between stopping and starting had been productively exhausted, making the pull-toward question a clean transition.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section turned on whether food preference is fixed or context-dependent — with the group ultimately landing on a productive both/and: preference is genuinely real and contextually formed at the same time. The sharper finding was the convergence across all five on a personal-stakes threshold: abstract environmental or social arguments won't move anyone; only something directly affecting their own life would tip the balance. That consensus was honest and largely unprompted.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The main moves were letting the Will–Amir disagreement develop before naming it, then using a single framing prompt to open it to the group — which brought in David's useful synthesis and Will's self-correction without moderator pressure. Drawing Ibrahim and Isaiah in by direct address after they'd been quiet worked cleanly; both gave substantive, honest answers. The closing synthesis-and-wrap timed well — the personal-stakes thread had reached natural exhaustion.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This closing section turned on the distinction between genuine preference and unexamined default — whether 'I don't want it' reflects actual deliberation or comfortable inertia. David's challenge to Amir's stated clarity produced a rare live shift: Amir visibly unsettled his own position mid-session. The section's sharpest finding was that 'picking a cleaner story' may be near-universal, and that honest uncertainty is harder to sustain than either conviction or open ambivalence.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The approach was minimal intervention — open floor, light affirmations, repeated invitation to Will, Ibrahim, and Isaiah who never took it. Letting David challenge Amir directly without moderator framing was the right call; the exchange was more productive than any prompt would have produced. The risk was that three participants went unheard at close. Whether that reflects genuine satisfaction or reluctance to complicate a strong finish is unresolved.

Hi everyone, welcome and thanks so much for joining today — really glad you're all here. My name's Alex, and I'll be facilitating the conversation. We've got about 45 minutes together, and the session will be recorded for research purposes, so just bear that in mind.

A few quick things before we get going. This is genuinely a conversation, not a quiz — there are no right or wrong answers, and I'm not looking for any particular response. What I'm interested in is what you actually think, what you've actually experienced, what you genuinely do in your own life. So the more specific and honest you can be, the more useful it is. If something someone else says connects with your own experience, feel free to jump in — you don't have to wait to be asked. And if you disagree with something, that's completely fine too — different views are just as useful as agreement.

Okay, let's start simple. Go ahead and say your name and where in the UK you're coming from today.
I'm David, I'm from Glasgow. Been here my whole life, actually.
Yeah, I'm Amir, I'm from Birmingham actually — so not too far from you in the grand scheme of things, David. West Midlands. Been here my whole life too, pretty much.
Right, I'm Will. I'm up in rural Scotland — much quieter than Glasgow, I'd say. Different world sometimes. Been here most of my life as well, so yeah, I'm settling in to the pace of it.

I'm Isaiah, I'm from the Leeds area actually — so yeah, Yorkshire. Urban setting, quite different from what you're describing, Will. I mean, Glasgow and Birmingham are proper cities like Leeds, but rural Scotland sounds like a completely different thing altogether. The pace, the access to stuff... I reckon that shapes how people eat and what they think about food quite a bit, doesn't it? Like, in the city you've got everything on your doorstep, takeaways, supermarkets, all that. Can't imagine what it's like trying to get fresh stuff regularly if you're in the middle of nowhere. Curious to hear how that actually works for you lot.

Well, it's actually not as bad as that makes it sound, to be honest. I mean, yeah, there's no Tesco on the corner, but that's kind of the point — you end up knowing the people who supply your food. I've got relationships with a couple of local farms, and I can get meat direct from them. It's fresher than anything you'd pick up in a supermarket, and I know where it's come from. There's a wee market that comes through, and you learn where the decent stuff is.

If anything, I'd say rural areas have an advantage sometimes. You're not relying on what the big chains decide to stock or how long it's been sitting in a distribution centre. You build networks with local suppliers. It takes a bit more effort, sure, but it's not like we're all surviving on tinned beans out here.
Good to hear from you, Will. Ibrahim, we haven't heard from you yet — whereabouts are you joining from?

I'm Ibrahim, I'm from the North East — Newcastle area. Urban, so yeah, more like what you're describing, Isaiah, with the supermarkets and that on every corner. Though I have to say, Will, what you're saying about knowing the farmers and getting stuff direct sounds pretty good actually. I don't really have that where I am. It's all just... you go to Sainsbury's or whatever, pick up what you need. Don't really think about it much beyond that, to be honest. But fair play to you for having those connections — that's kind of cool.

Great, welcome Ibrahim. Good to have you all here — Glasgow, Birmingham, Newcastle, Leeds, and rural Scotland. Quite a spread. Right, let's get into it properly. First thing I want to ask: what's your favourite place in your city — or your area — to spend time with your male friends? Could be a pub, someone's house, a park, anywhere. Why that place specifically?

For me, it's usually the pub, to be honest. There's a few we go to round Birmingham — nothing fancy, just places where you can grab a drink, have a laugh, catch the football on a screen if there's a match on. It's easy, innit. You don't have to plan much, just meet up after work or at the weekend, have a few pints, see who else is about. 

I mean, we'll do other stuff sometimes — go to someone's house, play some games, that sort of thing — but the pub's the default really. It's just where you go. Everyone knows the vibe, you're not at anyone's gaff so there's no mess to worry about, and you can stay as long as you want or bail whenever. Plus there's food, so you can grab something to eat if you're hungry.

Yeah, same here mate. The pub's just the easiest thing, innit. We've got a few locals round Newcastle we just end up in most weekends — grab a pint, watch the match if there's one on, chat shit basically. Don't need to organize anything fancy.

And you're right about the food — we'll usually get some chips or a burger or something while we're there. Nothing complicated. I'm not really fussed about what it is, just something to soak up the beer, you know? Some places do decent enough food, some are a bit dodgy, but you're not going there for Michelin stars or anything.

It's just the default really, like you say. Low effort, everyone knows what they're doing, you can just turn up.

Yeah, I get that — you're not going for the food obviously. But I'd say it does make a difference which pub you pick, even just for that side of it. Like, some places the burger's actually decent, and some places it's just... I don't know, grey and cold, you know? 

We've got one we go to fairly regularly where the chips are proper good — proper crispy, not soggy — and they do a decent burger. And then there's another one down the road where honestly the food's a bit grim, so we tend to just stick with pints and crisps there instead. It's not like we're choosing the pub based on the food quality or anything, but once you're there, if the food's decent it does make the night better. You're gonna eat something anyway, might as well be something that's actually alright.

Yeah, fair point actually. I mean, you notice it, don't you? Like, there's definitely a difference between a pub where the food's decent and one where it's just... yeah, grim. I've got one we go to pretty regularly where the burgers are actually alright, proper seasoned meat and that, and then there's another one where you're just eating something that tastes like nothing. 

And yeah, you're gonna eat something anyway while you're there, so might as well be something that doesn't taste like cardboard. It's not like we're basing the whole night around finding good food, but if you're already getting something to eat, you might as well enjoy it. Makes the night better, doesn't it.

Yeah, that's spot on actually. There's a massive difference between a burger that's been properly made and one that's just... I dunno, thrown together. I've got a couple of pubs round Leeds where they actually care about what goes into it — seasoning, how they cook it, that kind of thing — and you can taste it straight away. And then you go somewhere else and it's like, why did I even bother ordering this?

The thing is though, I reckon it comes down to whether the pub's actually bothering with it or not. Like, some places treat the food as an afterthought — just reheat something or whatever — and some places actually season the meat properly, get decent beef to start with. Makes all the difference. You're sat there for a few hours anyway, you're gonna order something, so yeah, might as well be something that's actually edible.

I think it's also harder in some places than others to get decent stuff in the first place. Like, in the city you've got more choice of suppliers, more competition, so the decent pubs have more reason to step up. But I'm curious Will — with your local farm connections you mentioned earlier, are the restaurants and pubs round you using that stuff? Or is it mostly just individuals getting direct from the farmers like you do?
Will — Isaiah's put that one to you. What's your take?

Yeah, good question. Honestly, it varies a lot. Some of the better places round here do try to source locally — there's a couple of restaurants that'll mention it on the menu, you know, "local beef" or whatever. But a lot of the pubs and smaller places, they're still going through the standard suppliers. Cost thing, I reckon. It's easier to just order from the big distributors than to build those relationships.

The thing is, if you're getting it direct like I do, it's actually often cheaper than what you'd pay in a restaurant anyway. But that's because there's no markup, no middle man. The pubs can't do that — they need to buy at a price that lets them resell at a profit.

Where I go, honestly, it's mostly just people doing what I do — buying direct from the farms, getting to know the farmers. There's a market, a few farm shops. But I think there's potential there for more restaurants to do it if they wanted to. It'd probably be good for them as a selling point, especially if they could actually charge a bit more because it's quality stuff. But yeah, most of the pubs round here are just... they do food, but it's not really the draw, you know? It's more about it being there if you want something.

Cheers Will. So we've got the pub as the go-to for most of you, and Will coming at it from a different angle with the farm shops and that direct network. Let's shift to something related — how do you actually decide what to eat, day to day? Not just when you're out, but in general — what drives those choices?

I mean, for me it's pretty straightforward — I just eat what I fancy, really. Some nights I'll do a bit of chicken, other nights I might have a steak or something, or fish if I'm in the mood. It's not like I'm planning it all out or anything.

I think it depends on what's easy as well. Like, if I'm working late, I'll just grab something quick — could be a burger, could be takeaway, doesn't really matter. If I've got a bit more time, maybe I'll actually cook something proper. There's a Tesco not far from me, so whatever I need's usually there.

Honestly though, I don't think about it that much. It's just what you fancy eating, innit? I'll have meat most days probably, but not because I'm thinking "oh, I need to eat meat" — it's just what I feel like having. Some people seem to make it a massive thing, but I don't really get it. You just eat what you want.

Yeah, that's a good point Will made about the markup. I've actually noticed that sometimes — like, you'll hear what someone's paying a farmer for beef, and then you see what a restaurant's charging for it, and it's mad, innit? The difference between what the person producing it gets and what you end up paying.

I mean, I'm not gonna pretend I'm thinking about that every time I grab something from Tesco, because honestly I'm not. But when you do notice it, it's a bit mad. Like, the farmer's getting paid next to nothing and then somehow it's fifteen quid for a burger on a menu.

That's probably why a lot of pubs just stick with the standard suppliers though — easier to know what you're gonna pay, easier to manage. Building those relationships like you're doing, Will, that takes time and effort that most places probably can't be bothered with. Even if it'd be better for them in the end.

Yeah, but that's kind of the thing though, isn't it? Like David, you're saying you don't think about it much, and fair enough — I get that. But then you're also noticing the markup and thinking it's mad when you do clock it. So it's there, you know?

I think the difference is, if you actually care about what you're eating — like, whether it's decent meat that's been looked after properly — then you do end up thinking about it a bit more. Not in like a preachy way, just... you notice when something's quality and when it's not. And that's what I was saying about the burgers — some pubs actually give a shit, and you can taste it. Other places, they're just shifting units.

The markup thing's interesting though. I mean, yeah, it's mad what restaurants charge versus what the farmer gets. But I reckon that's partly why the food can be dodgy sometimes — because they're buying cheap stuff to begin with to make their margin work. If you're paying shit to the farmer, you're getting shit product, and then you're trying to make that taste decent on a plate. Doesn't work, does it?

I'm not saying everyone's gotta be like Will with the farm connections — that's not practical for most people — but there's maybe a middle ground where you just... pick your spots? Go to places that actually seem to care about what they're serving, rather than just whatever's convenient.

Fair enough, yeah. You're right — I do notice it when I actually pay attention, I just don't think about it that often. That's different from not caring, I suppose.

And yeah, I get what you're saying about picking your spots. I mean, I'll go back to places where the food's decent, same as you lot. If a burger's actually good, you notice it, you remember it. I'm not gonna keep going somewhere that serves rubbish just because it's convenient.

I guess the difference is I'm not... I dunno, constantly evaluating where my food's come from or whatever. Like, if I'm at Tesco grabbing something quick on the way home from work, I'm just grabbing it. But if I'm going out somewhere, yeah, you'd rather go somewhere that's actually put thought into it.

It's just different headspaces though, innit? Going out is different from just feeding yourself on a Tuesday night. I don't need to overthink a weeknight dinner, but when you're going somewhere for a night out with mates, then fair play, might as well be somewhere decent.

Yeah, I hear you on that — weeknight versus going out is definitely different, and I'm not saying you need to be thinking deep about every meal. That'd be mental.

But I think the thing is, the habits you build on those Tuesday nights kind of feed into everything else, you know? Like, if you're always just grabbing whatever's quickest from Tesco without really clocking what it is, then that becomes normal. And then when you do go out, you're maybe less bothered about quality because that's just... how you eat?

Whereas if you're even slightly more aware on the weeknights — like, just picking something that's actually decent rather than the first thing that catches your eye — then when you're out, you're already in that headspace. You actually notice the difference between a good burger and a shit one because you're used to eating halfway decent stuff.

I'm not saying you've gotta spend an hour cooking every night or anything. Just... I dunno, even just knowing what you're grabbing tastes alright makes a difference. It's not overthinking it, it's just not completely switching your brain off about food, even when you're knackered on a Tuesday.

Yeah, that idea about habits stacking up is interesting — whether the defaults you build on a normal Tuesday actually shape how you eat more broadly. Good thread to have out there.

Let me take us somewhere that connects to a lot of what's just come up. You've been talking about what drives food choices — convenience, mood, quality, what context you're in. I want to push that a bit further: do you think being a man shapes what you eat? Not just in theory — but in practice, in your actual life. Does your gender influence what ends up on your plate?

Yeah, I reckon it does, but maybe not in the way people think. Like, there's definitely a thing about blokes just... not thinking about food as much? Not planning it out, not worrying about nutrition or whatever. You just eat what you fancy and don't make it a whole thing, innit. That's kind of what David was saying earlier — you just grab something.

But I don't think that's because we're hardwired to not care. I think it's more like... there's no pressure on you to care, so you don't bother. Whereas I reckon if you're a woman, you might feel like you've gotta think about it more — what's healthy, what's balanced, all that. For blokes it's just like, meat, bit of carbs, done.

The thing is though, I think that casual attitude can work against you sometimes. Like, if you're not thinking about what you're eating, you end up just eating whatever's easiest, and that's often not great. Which is maybe where that habit thing I was just saying comes in — you build these lazy defaults and then you're stuck with them.

I don't know if there's like a masculine thing about meat specifically though, the whole "real men eat meat" thing. That feels a bit... I dunno, forced? Like, yeah, most blokes I know eat meat, but I don't think they'd say it's because of being a man, you know? It's just what you eat. But maybe that's the point — it's so normal for us that we don't even notice it.
